solution: Only one person is chosen and there is no ordering, so this is a selection. "A girl or a boy" are mutually exclusive alternatives, so the addition principle applies. Number of ways \(= 30 + 20 = 50\). The monitor can be selected in 50 ways.

The two flags occupy an upper and a lower position, so the two flags are ORDERED (upper-red/lower-blue differs from upper-blue/lower-red). Only one flag of each colour exists, so no repetition. Upper position: 4 choices; lower position: 3 of the remaining flags. By the multiplication principle, number of signals \(= 4 \times 3 = 12\). 12 different signals can be generated.

SPACE has 5 distinct letters S, P, A, C, E. A two-letter "word" is an ordered pair of places, and here repetition is allowed, so each place can be filled independently. First letter: 5 ways; second letter: 5 ways. Number of words \(= 5 \times 5 = 25\). 25 two-letter words.
The two places are ordered, but now a letter once used cannot be repeated. First letter: 5 ways; second letter: the 4 remaining letters. Number of words \(= 5 \times 4 = 20\). 20 two-letter words.

The three places (hundreds, tens, units) are ordered and repetition is allowed. The hundreds place cannot be 0, or the number is not a three-digit number, so it has 4 choices from 1, 3, 5, 6. The tens and units places may take any of the 5 digits. Number of numbers \(= 4 \times 5 \times 5 = 100\). 100 three-digit numbers.

Ordered places, no repetition. Hundreds place: 4 choices (any of 1, 3, 5, 6, since 0 is not allowed as the leading digit). Tens place: 4 of the 5 digits remain, and 0 is now permitted. Units place: 3 digits remain. Number of numbers \(= 4 \times 4 \times 3 = 48\). 48 three-digit numbers.

The three places are ordered, repetition is allowed, and none of the digits 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 is 0, so there is no leading-digit restriction. Each of the three places can be filled in 5 ways. Number of numbers \(= 5 \times 5 \times 5 = 5^{3} = 125\). 125 three-digit numbers.

Each ring is set independently and its letter may repeat a letter on another ring, so the settings are ordered triples with repetition allowed. Total number of settings \(= 5 \times 5 \times 5 = 125\). Exactly one setting opens the lock, so in the worst case every other setting is tried first. Maximum number of false trials \(= 125 - 1 = 124\). 124 false trials.

Each of the 5 questions is answered independently in 2 ways (true or false), so the number of possible answer patterns is \(2^{5} = 32\). Every student's pattern is different, so the number of students is at most the number of patterns; and no student has the all-correct pattern, so that one pattern is unused. Number of students \(= 32 - 1 = 31\). 31 students appeared.

Numbers between 100 and 1000 are exactly the three-digit numbers. The units digit is fixed as 4, so it contributes 1 way. The hundreds digit can be any of \(1, 2, \ldots, 9\), i.e. 9 ways; the tens digit can be any of \(0, 1, \ldots, 9\), i.e. 10 ways. Number of such numbers \(= 9 \times 10 \times 1 = 90\). 90 numbers.

These are three-digit numbers, and the digit 7 must occupy exactly one of the three places, the other two places taking any digit other than 7. The three cases are mutually exclusive, so add them.
Case 1, 7 in the hundreds place: tens and units each have 9 choices (all digits except 7), giving \(9 \times 9 = 81\).
Case 2, 7 in the tens place: hundreds is from 1 to 9 excluding 7, i.e. 8 choices; units has 9 choices, giving \(8 \times 9 = 72\).
Case 3, 7 in the units place: hundreds 8 choices, tens 9 choices, giving \(8 \times 9 = 72\).
Total \(= 81 + 72 + 72 = 225\). 225 numbers.

A four-digit number is to be formed from the four digits 2, 3, 4, 7 without repetition, so all four digits are used and the numbers are simply the arrangements of these four distinct digits. Total number of such numbers \(= 4! = 24\). The largest arrangement is 7432 itself, so every one of these 24 numbers does not exceed 7432. Number of numbers \(= 24\).

Numbers of any length can be formed from 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 without repetition, so consider each length separately; the digits are all distinct and the arrangements are ordered.
One-digit and two-digit numbers are at most 65, so none exceeds 400.
Three-digit numbers exceeding 400 need the hundreds digit to be 4, 5 or 6, i.e. 3 choices, and then \(4 \times 3\) ways for the remaining two places: \(3 \times 4 \times 3 = 36\).
Every four-digit number exceeds 400: \(5 \times 4 \times 3 \times 2 = 120\).
Every five-digit number exceeds 400: \(5! = 120\).
Total \(= 36 + 120 + 120 = 276\). 276 numbers exceed 400.

The digits available are 0, 1, 2, 5, 7, 8 and repetition is allowed. A number strictly between 13 and 1000 has two or three digits.
Three-digit numbers: the leading digit cannot be 0, so 5 choices, and the other two places have 6 choices each, giving \(5 \times 6 \times 6 = 180\). All of these lie between 100 and 999, hence all are counted.
Two-digit numbers: leading digit 5 choices, units digit 6 choices, giving \(5 \times 6 = 30\). Of these, those not exceeding 13 are 10, 11 and 12 (13 itself cannot be formed, as 3 is not available), i.e. 3 numbers, which must be discarded: \(30 - 3 = 27\).
Total \(= 180 + 27 = 207\). 207 numbers.
The journey has two independent stages: choosing a gate, then choosing a staircase. Gate: 3 ways; staircase: 4 ways. By the multiplication principle, number of ways \(= 3 \times 4 = 12\). 12 ways.

Five of the six digits 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 are arranged with no repetition, and the number is divisible by 5, so the units digit is 0 or 5. These two cases are mutually exclusive.
Case 1, units digit 0: the remaining four places are filled by 4 of the digits 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, none of which is 0, so there is no leading-digit restriction: \(5 \times 4 \times 3 \times 2 = 120\).
Case 2, units digit 5: the remaining four places take 4 of the digits 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, giving \(5 \times 4 \times 3 \times 2 = 120\) arrangements, of which those beginning with 0 are not five-digit numbers and number \(4 \times 3 \times 2 = 24\); so \(120 - 24 = 96\).
Total \(= 120 + 96 = 216\). 216 numbers.
